**Uruguay**,<sup>[\[d\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-18)</sup> officially the **Oriental Republic of Uruguay**,<sup>[\[e\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-19)</sup> is a country in southeastern [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America). It shares borders with [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina) to its west and southwest and [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil) to its north and northeast, while bordering the [Río de la Plata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Río_de_la_Plata) to the south and the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean) to the southeast. It is part of the [Southern Cone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Cone) region of South America. Uruguay covers an area of approximately 176,215 square kilometers (68,037 sq mi).<sup>[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Uruguay_Presidencia-13)</sup> It has a population of almost 3.5 million people, of whom nearly 2 million live in [the metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevideo_metropolitan_area) of its capital and [largest city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Uruguay), [Montevideo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevideo).

The area that became Uruguay was first inhabited by groups of [hunter gatherers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunter_gatherer) 13,000 years ago.<sup>[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-archivo.presidencia.gub.uy-20)</sup> The first European explorer to reach the region was [Juan Díaz de Solís](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Díaz_de_Solís) in 1516, but the area was colonised later than its neighbours. At the time of [European arrival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_colonization_of_the_Americas), the [Charrúa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charrúa) were the predominant tribe, alongside other groups such as the [Guaraní](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guaraní_people) and the [Chaná](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaná_people). However, none of these peoples were socially or politically organised in large groups, which contributed to their decline.<sup>[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-21)</sup> Amid territorial disputes, the Portuguese established [Colônia do Sacramento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonia_del_Sacramento) in 1680, and the Spanish founded [Montevideo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevideo) as a military stronghold. Uruguay secured its independence between 1811 and 1828, following a four-way struggle involving Portugal, Spain, and later the [United Provinces of the Río de la Plata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Provinces_of_the_Río_de_la_Plata) and the [Empire of Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Brazil). In 1830, the country enacted its [constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Uruguay) and was formally established as an independent state.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-10-22)

Following independence, Uruguay experienced foreign intervention, internal conflicts and political instability.<sup>[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-23)</sup> From the second half of the 19th century, successive [waves of European migration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration_to_Uruguay), particularly from [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Uruguayans), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Uruguayans) and [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Uruguayans), reshaped the country's demographics and contributed to the development of modern [Uruguayan culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_Uruguay).[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-24)<sup>[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-25)</sup> During this period, national politics were dominated by the [Colorado Party](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Party_(Uruguay)>) and the [National Party](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Party_(Uruguay)>), collectively known as the Traditional Parties, which fought several civil wars.<sup>[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-26)</sup> In the early 20th century, a series of economic, labour and social reforms, combined with sustained political stability, established Uruguay as an advanced [welfare state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welfare_state) and earned it the nickname "Switzerland of the Americas".[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-27)

Economic crises and escalating political and social tensions amid the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War), including the activities of the far-left [National Liberation Movement–Tupamaros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tupamaros), an urban guerrilla movement, contributed to the erosion of democratic institutions in the late 1960s and early 1970s. This culminated in the [1973 coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_Uruguayan_coup_d'état), which ushered in a [civic-military dictatorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civic-military_dictatorship_of_Uruguay) that lasted until 1985.<sup>[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-28)</sup> Since the restoration of democracy, Uruguay has been a [constitutional republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic), with a president who serves as both [head of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_state) and [head of government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_government).

Uruguay is highly ranked in international measurements of democracy, government transparency, economic freedom, social progress, [income equality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_income_equality), [per capita income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_capita_income), innovation, and infrastructure.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-photos.state.gov-29)<sup>[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-30)</sup> It is classified as a [high-income economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank_high-income_economy). It is also highly [socially liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_liberalism), and has [fully legalised cannabis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Uruguay)—the first country in the world to do so—as well as [same-sex marriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage_in_Uruguay), [abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_in_Uruguay) and [euthanasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euthanasia_in_Uruguay).[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-31)<sup>[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-32)</sup> Uruguay is also a founding member of the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations), the [OAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organization_of_American_States), and [Mercosur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercosur).

The country of *Uruguay* takes its name from the [Río Uruguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruguay_River) in the [Indigenous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_in_Uruguay) [Guaraní](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guarani_languages) language. There are several interpretations, including "bird-river" ("the river of the *[uru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spot-winged_wood_quail)*", via [Charruan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charruan_languages), *urú* being a [common noun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_noun) for any wild fowl).[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-33)<sup>[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-34)</sup> The name could also refer to a river snail called *uruguá* (*[Pomella](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomella_(gastropod)>) megastoma*) that was plentiful across its shores.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-ElPaisName2012-35)

One of the most popular interpretations of the name was proposed by the renowned Uruguayan poet [Juan Zorrilla de San Martín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Zorrilla_de_San_Martín), "the river of painted birds";<sup>[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-ElPaisName2012-35)</sup> this interpretation, although dubious, still holds an important cultural significance in the country.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-36)

In Spanish colonial times and for some time thereafter, Uruguay and some neighbouring territories were called *[Banda Oriental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banda_Oriental) \[del Uruguay\]* ("Eastern Bank \[of the Uruguay River\]"), then for a few years the *[Provincia Oriental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provincia_Oriental)* ("Eastern Province").

Since its independence, the country has been known as "*República Oriental del Uruguay*", which literally translates to "*Republic East of the Uruguay* \[River\]". However, it is officially translated either as the "*Oriental Republic of Uruguay*"[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-CIA-37)<sup>[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-britannica-38)</sup> or the "*Eastern Republic of Uruguay*".[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-39)

Human presence in the region now known as Uruguay dates back approximately 13,000 years, with evidence of [hunter-gatherer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunter-gatherer) communities.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-archivo.presidencia.gub.uy-20)<sup>[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-40)</sup> It is estimated that at the time of the first contact with Europeans in the 16th century, there were about 9,000 [Charrúa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charrúa) and 6,000 [Chaná](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaná_people) and some [Guaraní](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guaraní_people) island settlements.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-41)

There is an extensive archaeological collection of man-made [tumuli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumulus) known as "*[Cerritos de Indios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerritos_de_Indios)*" in the eastern part of the country, some of them dating back to 5,000 years ago. Very little is known about the people who built them as they left no written record, but evidence has been found in place of indigenous agriculture and of extinct [indigenous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American_dogs) woolly dogs.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-42)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-43)[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-44)

The [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_discoveries) were the first Europeans to enter the region of present-day Uruguay in 1512.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Spate-45)<sup>[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-46)</sup> The [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire) arrived in present-day Uruguay in 1515 but were the first to set foot in the area, claiming it for the crown.<sup>[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-dept-state-47)</sup> The indigenous peoples' fierce resistance to [conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_colonization_of_the_Americas), combined with the absence of valuable resources, limited European settlement in the region during the 16th and 17th centuries.<sup>[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-dept-state-47)</sup> Uruguay then became a zone of contention between the Spanish and Portuguese empires. In 1603, the Spanish began introducing cattle, which became a source of regional wealth. The first permanent Spanish settlement was founded in 1624 at [Soriano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villa_Soriano) on the [Río Negro](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Río_Negro_(Uruguay)>). In 1680, the Portuguese built a fort at [Colonia del Sacramento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonia_del_Sacramento).[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-48)

[Montevideo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevideo), the current capital of Uruguay, was founded by the Spanish in 1726 as a military stronghold.<sup>[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-:1-49)</sup> Its natural harbour soon developed into a commercial area competing with [Río de la Plata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceroyalty_of_the_Río_de_la_Plata)'s capital, [Buenos Aires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buenos_Aires).[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-dept-state-47)<sup>[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-:1-49)</sup> Uruguay's early 19th-century history was shaped by ongoing fights for dominance in the [Platine region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Plata_Basin)<sup>[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-dept-state-47)</sup> between British, Spanish, Portuguese, and other colonial forces. In 1806 and 1807, the [British army attempted to seize Buenos Aires and Montevideo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_invasions_of_the_Río_de_la_Plata) as part of the [Napoleonic Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleonic_Wars).<sup>[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-:2-50)</sup> Montevideo was occupied by British forces from February to September 1807.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-:2-50)

In 1811, [José Gervasio Artigas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/José_Gervasio_Artigas), who became Uruguay's national hero, launched a successful revolt against the [Spanish authorities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceroyalty_of_the_Río_de_la_Plata), defeating them on 18 May at the [Battle of Las Piedras](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Las_Piedras_(1811)>).<sup>[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-dept-state-47)</sup> In 1813, the new government in Buenos Aires convened a constituent assembly where Artigas emerged as a champion of federalism, demanding political and economic autonomy for each area and the [Banda Oriental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banda_Oriental) in particular.<sup>[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-3-51)</sup> The assembly refused to seat the delegates from the Banda Oriental; however, Buenos Aires pursued a system based on unitary centralism.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-3-51)

As a result, Artigas broke with Buenos Aires and besieged Montevideo, taking the city in early 1815.<sup>[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-3-51)</sup> Once the troops from Buenos Aires had withdrawn, the Banda Oriental appointed its first autonomous government.<sup>[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-3-51)</sup> Artigas organised the [Federal League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liga_Federal) under his protection, consisting of six provinces, five of which later became part of Argentina.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-3-51)

In 1816, 10,000 Portuguese troops invaded the Banda Oriental from Brazil; they took Montevideo in January 1817.<sup>[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-3-51)</sup> After nearly four more years of struggle, the [Portuguese Kingdom of Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Portugal,_Brazil_and_the_Algarves) annexed the *Banda Oriental* as a province under the name of "[Cisplatina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cisplatina)".<sup>[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-3-51)</sup> The [Brazilian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Brazil) became independent of Portugal in 1822. In response to the annexation, the [Thirty-Three Orientals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty-Three_Orientals), led by [Juan Antonio Lavalleja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Antonio_Lavalleja), declared independence on 25 August 1825, supported by the [United Provinces of the Río de la Plata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Provinces_of_the_Río_de_la_Plata) (present-day Argentina).<sup>[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-dept-state-47)</sup> This led to the 500-day-long [Cisplatine War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cisplatine_War). Neither side gained the upper hand, and in 1828, the [Treaty of Montevideo](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Montevideo_(1828)>), fostered by the United Kingdom through the diplomatic efforts of [Viscount John Ponsonby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ponsonby,_1st_Viscount_Ponsonby), gave birth to Uruguay as an independent state. 25 August is celebrated as Independence Day, a [national holiday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_holidays_in_Uruguay).<sup>[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-52)</sup> The nation's [first constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Uruguay) was adopted on 18 July 1830.<sup>[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-dept-state-47)</sup> The country was officially the Oriental State of Uruguay.

At the time of independence, Uruguay had an estimated population of just under 75,000.<sup>[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-5-53)</sup> The political scene in Uruguay became split between two parties: the conservative *[Blancos](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Party_(Uruguay)>)* (Whites), headed by the second President [Manuel Oribe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Oribe), representing the agricultural interests of the countryside, and the liberal *[Colorados](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Party_(Uruguay)>)* (Reds), led by the first President [Fructuoso Rivera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fructuoso_Rivera), representing the business interests of Montevideo. The Uruguayan parties received support from warring political factions in neighbouring [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina), which became involved in Uruguayan affairs.

The *Colorados* favoured the exiled Argentine liberal [Unitarios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitarian_Party), many of whom had taken refuge in Montevideo, while the Blanco president Manuel Oribe was a close friend of the Argentine ruler [Manuel de Rosas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_de_Rosas). On 15 June 1838, an army led by the Colorado leader Rivera overthrew President Oribe, who fled to Argentina.<sup>[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-5-53)</sup> Rivera declared war on Rosas in 1839. The conflict would last 13 years and become known as the [Guerra Grande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruguayan_Civil_War) (the Great War).<sup>[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-5-53)</sup> In 1843, an Argentine army overran Uruguay on Oribe's behalf but failed to take the capital. The [siege of Montevideo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruguayan_Civil_War#The_Great_Siege) began in February 1843 and lasted nine years.<sup>[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-6-54)</sup> The besieged Uruguayans called on resident foreigners for help, which led to a French and an Italian legion being formed, the latter led by the exiled [Giuseppe Garibaldi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Garibaldi).[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-6-54)

In 1845, Britain and France intervened against Rosas to restore commerce to normal levels in the region. Their efforts proved ineffective, and by 1849, tired of the war, both withdrew after signing a treaty favourable to Rosas.<sup>[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-6-54)</sup> It appeared that Montevideo would finally fall when an uprising against Rosas, led by [Justo José de Urquiza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justo_José_de_Urquiza), governor of Argentina's [Entre Ríos Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entre_Ríos_Province), began. The Brazilian intervention in May 1851 on behalf of the *Colorados*, combined with the uprising, changed the situation, and Oribe was defeated. The siege of Montevideo was lifted, and the *Guerra Grande* finally came to an end.<sup>[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-6-54)</sup> Montevideo rewarded Brazil's support by signing treaties that confirmed Brazil's right to intervene in Uruguay's internal affairs.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-6-54)

In accordance with the 1851 treaties, Brazil intervened militarily in Uruguay as often as it deemed necessary.<sup>[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-7-55)</sup> In 1865, the [Triple Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_the_Triple_Alliance) was formed by the [emperor of Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_of_Brazil), the [president of Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Argentina), and the Colorado general [Venancio Flores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venancio_Flores), the Uruguayan head of government whom they both had helped to gain power. The Triple Alliance declared war on the Paraguayan leader [Francisco Solano López](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Solano_López).<sup>[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-7-55)</sup> The resulting [Paraguayan War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguayan_War) ended with the invasion of Paraguay and its defeat by the armies of the three countries. Montevideo was used as a supply station by the Brazilian navy, and it experienced a period of prosperity and relative calm during the war.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-7-55)

The first railway line was assembled in Uruguay in 1867, and a branch consisting of a horse-drawn train was opened. The present-day [State Railways Administration of Uruguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Railways_Administration_of_Uruguay) maintains 2,900 km (1,800 mi) of extendable railway network.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-56)

The constitutional government of General [Lorenzo Batlle y Grau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorenzo_Batlle_y_Grau) (1868–72) suppressed the [Revolution of the Lances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolution_of_the_Lances) by the [Blancos](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Party_(Uruguay)>).<sup>[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-9-57)</sup> After two years of struggle, a peace agreement was signed in 1872 that gave the Blancos a share in the emoluments and functions of government through control of four of the [departments of Uruguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_Uruguay).<sup>[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-9-57)</sup> This establishment of the policy of co-participation represented the search for a new formula of compromise based on the coexistence of the party in power and the opposition party.<sup>[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-9-57)</sup> Despite this agreement, the Colorado rule was threatened by the failed [Tricolor Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tricolor_Revolution?action=edit&redlink=1) in 1875 and the Revolution of the [Quebracho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebracho,_Uruguay) in 1886.

The Colorado effort to reduce Blancos to only three departments caused a Blanco uprising of 1897, which ended with creating 16 departments, of which the Blancos now had control over six. Blancos were given ⅓ seats in Congress.<sup>[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-58)</sup> This division of power lasted until President [Jose Batlle y Ordonez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Batlle_y_Ordonez) instituted his political reforms, which caused the last uprising by Blancos in 1904 that ended with the [Battle of Masoller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Masoller) and the death of Blanco leader [Aparicio Saravia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aparicio_Saravia).

Between 1875 and 1890, the centre of power shifted toward the military.<sup>[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-10-22)</sup> During this authoritarian period, the government took steps toward the organisation of the country as a modern state, encouraging its economic and social transformation. Pressure groups (consisting mainly of businessmen, *[hacendados](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hacendado)*, and industrialists) were organised and had a strong influence on the government.<sup>[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-10-22)</sup> A transition period (1886–90) followed, during which politicians began recovering lost ground, and some civilian participation in government occurred.<sup>[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-10-22)</sup> After the [Guerra Grande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruguayan_Civil_War), there was a sharp rise in the number of immigrants, primarily from Italy and Spain. By 1879, the total population of the country was over 438,500.<sup>[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-8-59)</sup> The economy reflected a steep upswing (if demonstrated graphically, above all other related economic determinants) in livestock raising and exports.<sup>[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-8-59)</sup> Montevideo became a major financial centre of the region and an [entrepôt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entrepôt) for goods from Argentina, Brazil, and Paraguay.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-8-59)

The Colorado leader [José Batlle y Ordóñez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/José_Batlle_y_Ordóñez) was elected president in 1903.<sup>[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-12-60)</sup> The following year, the Blancos led a rural revolt, and eight bloody months of fighting ensued before their leader, [Aparicio Saravia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aparicio_Saravia), was killed in battle. Government forces emerged victorious, leading to the end of the co-participation politics that had begun in 1872.<sup>[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-12-60)</sup> Batlle had two terms (1903–07 and 1911–15) during which he instituted major reforms, such as a welfare program, government participation in the economy, and a plural executive.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-dept-state-47)

[Gabriel Terra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Terra) became president in March 1931. His inauguration coincided with the effects of the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression),<sup>[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-14-61)</sup> and the social climate became tense as a result of the lack of jobs. There were confrontations in which police and leftists died.<sup>[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-14-61)</sup> In 1933, Terra organised a coup d'état, dissolving the General Assembly and governing by decree.<sup>[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-14-61)</sup> A new constitution was promulgated in 1934, transferring powers to the president.<sup>[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-14-61)</sup> In general, the Terra government weakened or neutralised economic nationalism and social reform.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-14-61)

In 1938, general elections were held, and Terra's brother-in-law, General [Alfredo Baldomir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfredo_Baldomir), was elected president. Under pressure from organised labour and the National Party, Baldomir advocated free elections, freedom of the press, and a new constitution.<sup>[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-15-62)</sup> Although Baldomir declared Uruguay neutral in 1939, British warships and the German ship [*Admiral Graf Spee*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_cruiser_Admiral_Graf_Spee) fought [a battle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_River_Plate) not far off Uruguay's coast.<sup>[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-15-62)</sup> The *Admiral Graf Spee* took refuge in [Montevideo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevideo), claiming sanctuary in a neutral port, but was later ordered out.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-15-62)

In 1945, Uruguay formally signed the [Declaration by the United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_by_United_Nations) and entered [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II), leading the country to declare war on [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany) and [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Japan). Following the end of the war, it became a founding member of the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations).

An armed group of [Marxist–Leninist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxism–Leninism) urban guerrillas, known as the [Tupamaros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tupamaros), emerged in the 1960s, engaging in activities such as bank robbery, kidnapping, and assassination, in addition to attempting an overthrow of the government.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-63)[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-64)

President [Jorge Pacheco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Pacheco_Areco) declared a state of emergency in 1968, followed by a further suspension of civil liberties in 1972. In 1973, amid increasing economic and political turmoil, the armed forces, asked by President [Juan María Bordaberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_María_Bordaberry), disbanded Parliament and established a [civilian-military regime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civic-military_dictatorship_of_Uruguay).<sup>[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-dept-state-47)</sup> The [CIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency)-backed campaign of political repression and state terror involving intelligence operations and assassination of opponents was called [Operation Condor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Condor).[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-65)[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-66)

According to one source, around 180 Uruguayans are known to have been killed and disappeared, with thousands more illegally detained and tortured during the 12-year civil-military rule from 1973 to 1985.<sup>[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-67)</sup> Most were killed in Argentina and other neighbouring countries, with 36 of them having been killed in Uruguay.<sup>[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-68)</sup> According to Edy Kaufman (cited by David Altman),<sup>[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-69)</sup> Uruguay at the time had the highest per capita number of political prisoners in the world. "Kaufman, who spoke at the U.S. Congressional Hearings of 1976 on behalf of [Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International), estimated that one in every five Uruguayans went into exile, one in fifty were detained, and one in five hundred went to prison (most of them tortured)." Social spending was reduced, and many state-owned companies were privatised. However, the economy did not improve and deteriorated after 1980; the [gross domestic product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_domestic_product) (GDP) fell by 20%, and unemployment rose to 17%. The state intervened by trying to bail out failing companies and banks.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-70)<sup>: 45</sup> 

A new constitution, drafted by the military, was rejected in a November 1980 referendum.<sup>[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-dept-state-47)</sup> Following the referendum, the armed forces announced a plan for the return to civilian rule, and national elections were held in 1984.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-dept-state-47)[Colorado Party](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Party_(Uruguay)>) leader [Julio María Sanguinetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julio_María_Sanguinetti) won the presidency and served from 1985 to 1990. The first Sanguinetti administration implemented economic reforms and consolidated democracy following the country's years under military rule.<sup>[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-dept-state-47)</sup> The National Party's [Luis Alberto Lacalle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Alberto_Lacalle) won the 1989 presidential election, and a referendum endorsed amnesty for human rights abusers. Sanguinetti was then reelected in 1994.<sup>[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-71)</sup> Both presidents continued the economic structural reforms initiated after the reinstatement of democracy.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-72)

The 1999 national elections were held under a new electoral system established by a 1996 constitutional amendment.<sup>[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-73)</sup> Colorado Party candidate [Jorge Batlle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Batlle), aided by the support of the National Party, defeated [Broad Front](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broad_Front_(Uruguay)>) candidate [Tabaré Vázquez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabaré_Vázquez). The formal coalition ended in November 2002, when the Blancos withdrew their ministers from the cabinet,<sup>[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-dept-state-47)</sup> although the Blancos continued to support the Colorados on most issues. Low commodity prices and economic difficulties in Uruguay's main export markets (starting in Brazil with the devaluation of the [real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazilian_real), then in [Argentina in 2002](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentine_economic_crisis_(1999–2002)>)) caused a severe recession; the economy contracted by 11%, unemployment climbed to 21%, and the percentage of Uruguayans in poverty rose to over 30%.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-cong-r-74)

In 2004, Uruguayans elected [Tabaré Vázquez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabaré_Vázquez) as president while giving the Broad Front a majority in both houses of Parliament.<sup>[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-75)</sup> Vázquez stuck to economic orthodoxy. As commodity prices soared and the economy recovered from the recession, he tripled foreign investment, cut poverty and unemployment, cut [public debt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_debt) from 79% of GDP to 60%, and kept inflation steady.<sup>[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-76)</sup> In 2009, [José Mujica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/José_Mujica), a former left-wing guerrilla leader (Tupamaros) who spent almost 15 years in prison during the country's military rule, emerged as the new president as the Broad Front won the election for a second time.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-77)[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-78)[Abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_in_Uruguay) was legalised in 2012,<sup>[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-79)</sup> followed by [same-sex marriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage_in_Uruguay)<sup>[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-80)</sup> and [cannabis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legality_of_cannabis_in_Uruguay) in the following year,<sup>[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-81)</sup> making Uruguay the first country in the modern era to legalise cannabis.

In 2014, Tabaré Vázquez was elected to a non-consecutive second presidential term, which began on 1 March 2015.<sup>[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-82)</sup> In 2020, after 15 years of left-wing rule, he was succeeded by [Luis Alberto Lacalle Pou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Alberto_Lacalle_Pou), a member of the conservative [National Party](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Party_(Uruguay)>), as the 42nd President of Uruguay.<sup>[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-83)</sup> On 1 March 2025, [Yamandu Orsi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamandú_Orsi) took office as Uruguay's new president, as the left-wing coalition of the Broad Front returned to power after a five-year interruption.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-84)

With 176,214 km<sup>2</sup> (68,037 sq mi) of continental land and 125,436 km<sup>2</sup> (48,431 sq mi) of [territorial waters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territorial_waters),<sup>[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-encifras-85)</sup> Uruguay is the second-smallest sovereign nation in South America (after [Suriname](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suriname)) and the third smallest territory ([French Guiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Guiana) is the smallest).<sup>[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-CIA-37)</sup> The landscape features mostly rolling plains and low hill ranges (*cuchillas*) with a fertile coastal lowland.<sup>[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-CIA-37)</sup> Uruguay has 660 km (410 mi) of [coastline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coastline_paradox).<sup>[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-CIA-37)</sup> The highest point in the country is the [Cerro Catedral](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Catedral_(Uruguay)>), whose peak reaches 514 m (1,686 ft) [AMSL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Above_mean_sea_level) in the *Sierra Carapé* hill range. To the southwest is the [Río de la Plata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Río_de_la_Plata), the estuary of the Uruguay River (the river which forms the country's western border).

A dense fluvial network covers the country, consisting of four river basins, or deltas: the [Río de la Plata Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Río_de_la_Plata_Basin), the [Uruguay River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruguay_River), the [Laguna Merín](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagoa_Mirim), and the Río Negro. The major internal river is the [Río Negro](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Río_Negro_(Uruguay)>) ("Black River"), dammed in 1945, resulting in the formation of the artificial [Rincón del Bonete Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rincón_del_Bonete_Lake) in the heart of Uruguay. Several lagoons are found along the Atlantic coast.

Montevideo is the southernmost national capital in the Americas and the third most southerly in the world (after [Canberra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canberra) and [Wellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellington)). Uruguay is the only country in South America situated entirely south of the [Tropic of Capricorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropic_of_Capricorn), and is the southernmost sovereign state in the world when ordered by northernmost point of latitude. There are ten [national parks in Uruguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_parks_of_Uruguay): Five in the wetland areas of the east, three in the central hill country, and one in the west along the Rio Uruguay. Uruguay is home to the [Uruguayan savanna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruguayan_savanna) terrestrial ecoregion.<sup>[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-DinersteinOlson2017-86)</sup> The country had a 2019 [Forest Landscape Integrity Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Landscape_Integrity_Index) mean score of 3.61/10, ranking it 147th globally out of 172 countries.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-FLII-Supplementary-87)

Located entirely within the southern temperate zone, Uruguay has a climate that is relatively mild and fairly uniform nationwide.<sup>[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-27-88)</sup> According to the [Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Köppen_climate_classification), most of the country has a [humid subtropical climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_subtropical_climate) (Cfa). Only in some spots of the Atlantic Coast and at the summit of the highest hills of the [Cuchilla Grande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuchilla_Grande) is the climate [oceanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_climate) (Cfb).

The country experiences four seasons, with summer from December to March and winter from June to September. Seasonal variations are pronounced, but extremes in temperature are rare.<sup>[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-27-88)</sup> Summers are tempered by winds off the Atlantic, and severe cold in winter is unknown.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-27-88)<sup>[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-89)</sup> Although it never gets too cold, frosts occur every year during the winter months, and precipitation such as sleet and hail occur almost every winter, but snow is very rare; it does occur every couple of years at higher elevations, but almost always without accumulation. As would be expected with its abundance of water, high humidity and fog are common.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-27-88)

The absence of mountains, which act as weather barriers, makes all locations vulnerable to high winds and rapid changes in weather as fronts or storms sweep across the country.<sup>[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-loc-27-88)</sup> These storms can be strong; they can bring [squalls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squall), [hail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hail), and sometimes even [tornadoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado).<sup>[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-90)</sup> The country experiences [extratropical cyclones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extratropical_cyclone) but no tropical cyclones, due to the fact that the [South Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean) is rarely warm enough for their development. Both summer and winter weather may vary from day to day with the passing of storm fronts, where a hot northerly wind may occasionally be followed by a cold wind ([pampero](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pampero_(wind)>)) from the Argentine [Pampas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pampas).[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-britannica-38)

Even though both temperature and precipitation are quite uniform nationwide, there are considerable differences across the territory. The average annual temperature of the country is 17.5 °C (63.5 °F), ranging from 16 °C (61 °F) in the southeast to 19 °C (66 °F) in the northwest.<sup>[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-inumet.gub.uy-91)</sup> Winter temperatures range from a daily average of 11 °C (52 °F) in the south to 14 °C (57 °F) in the north, while summer average daily temperatures range from 21 °C (70 °F) in the southeast to 25 °C (77 °F) in the northwest.<sup>[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-92)</sup> The southeast is considerably cooler than the rest of the country, especially during spring, when the ocean with cold water after the winter cools down the temperature of the air and brings more humidity to that region. However, the south of the country receives less precipitation than the north. For example, Montevideo receives approximately 1,100 mm (43 in) of precipitation per year, while the city of Rivera in the northeast receives 1,600 mm (63 in).<sup>[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-inumet.gub.uy-91)</sup> The heaviest precipitation occurs during the autumn months, although more frequent rainy spells occur in winter.<sup>[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-britannica-38)</sup> But periods of drought or excessive rain can occur anytime during the year.

National extreme temperatures at sea level are 44 °C (111 °F) in [Paysandú](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paysandú) city (20 January 1943) and [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida,_Uruguay) city (14 January 2022)<sup>[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-93)</sup> and −11.0 °C (12.2 °F) in [Melo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melo,_Uruguay) city (14 June 1967).[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-94)

Uruguay is a [representative democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representative_democracy) republic with a [presidential system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_system).<sup>[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-biz-guide-95)</sup> The Uruguayan Constitution establishes a [separation of powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_of_powers) intended to provide a system of [checks and balances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checks_and_balances) and members of government are elected for a five-year term by a [universal suffrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_suffrage) system.<sup>[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-biz-guide-95)</sup> Uruguay is a [unitary state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_state): justice, education, health, security, foreign policy and defence are all administered nationwide.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-biz-guide-95)

The Executive branch is exercised by the [president of the Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Uruguay) who serves both as [head of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_state) and [head of government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_government), along with a [Council of Ministers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_Uruguay) of 14 [members](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ministries_of_Uruguay).<sup>[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-biz-guide-95)</sup> Together with the [Vice-President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_Uruguay), the President is elected through a direct popular vote for a five-year term, with no possibility of immediate re-election. Each party presents a single presidential ticket—determined through primary elections—and the winning ticket must receive an absolute majority of votes.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-:02-96)

The Legislative branch is constituted by the [General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Assembly_of_Uruguay), a [bicameral legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicameral_legislature) made up of the [Chamber of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamber_of_Deputies_of_Uruguay) and the [Chamber of Senators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Uruguay). The former consists of 99 members representing the 19 departments, elected for a five-year term based on proportional representation, while the latter comprises 31 members—30 elected for five-year terms by proportional representation—and the Vice-President, who presides over the chamber and has the right to vote.<sup>[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-biz-guide-95)</sup> Parliamentary elections are held jointly with the presidential election in a general vote.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-:02-96)
